blocks.task_summary: Find the coordinates of points on y = e^(cos 2x), −π/4 ≤ x ≤ π, where the gradient is zero.
method_path: apply chain rule to differentiate f(x) = e^(cos 2x)
set f'(x) = −2 sin 2x e^(cos 2x) = 0
solve sin 2x = 0 for x in [−π/4, π]
find corresponding y-coordinates
state three coordinate pairs: (0, e), (π/2, 1/e), (π, e)

evidence.basis: (M1) attempt to use chain rule to find f′(x); f′(x) = −2 sin 2x e^(cos2x) A1; (M1) sin 2x = 0; 2x = 0, π, 2π, … ; x = 0, π/2, π, … A1; Coordinates are (0,e), (π/2, 1/e), (π,e) A1. Special case note: for two correct coordinate pairs award (M1)A1(M1)A0A1; for extra coordinate pairs award (M1)A1(M1)A1A0.

blocks.task_summary: Using the second derivative at each stationary point, show that the curve has two local maximum points and one local minimum point.
method_path: differentiate f'(x) using product rule to obtain f''(x)
evaluate f''(x) at x = 0, π/2, π
classify: f''(0) = −4e < 0 → local maximum
classify: f''(π) = −4e < 0 → local maximum
classify: f''(π/2) = 4/e > 0 → local minimum

evidence.basis: (M1) attempt to differentiate f′(x) using product rule; f′′(x) = (−2 sin 2x)(−2 sin 2x)e^(cos2x) − 4 cos 2x e^(cos2x) A1; at x = 0, f′′(x) = −4e < 0 so maximum AND at x = π, f′′(x) = −4e < 0 so maximum R1; at x = π/2, f′′(x) = 4/e > 0 so minimum R1. Note: values for second derivative must be correct to award R marks.

blocks.task_summary: Sketch the curve y = f(x) for 0 ≤ x ≤ π, taking into consideration the relative values of the second derivative found in part (b).
method_path: plot maxima at (0, e) and (π, e)
plot minimum at (π/2, 1/e)
draw smooth curve with correct general shape
show higher rate of change of gradient (sharper curvature) at maxima
show lower rate of change of gradient (gentler curvature) at minimum

evidence.basis: A1A1A1. Award A1 for general shape, A1 for correct maxima (0,e), (π,e) and minimum point (π/2, 1/e) and A1 for showing a higher rate of change of gradient at maxima and a lower rate of change of gradient at the minimum point.

blocks.task_summary: Find the Maclaurin series for cos 2x, then for e^(cos 2x − 1), then for f(x) = e^(cos 2x), each up to and including the term in x⁴.
method_path: (i) write standard Maclaurin series for cos θ, substitute θ = 2x: cos 2x = 1 − 2x² + (2/3)x⁴ + …
(ii) substitute series for cos 2x − 1 into series for e^θ and expand: e^(cos2x−1) = 1 − 2x² + (8/3)x⁴ + …
(iii) multiply by e: f(x) = e − 2ex² + (8e/3)x⁴ + …
accepted_alternatives: Method 2 (markscheme page 23): express e^(cos2x−1) = e^(−2x²) · e^(2x⁴/3), find series for each factor separately, then multiply to obtain the same result.

evidence.basis: (ii) METHOD 1: (M1) attempt to substitute series for cos2x−1 into series for e^x; A1 for correct substitution; e^(cos2x−1) = 1 + (−2x² + (2/3)x⁴) + (1/2)(−2x² + …)² + … = 1 − 2x² + (8/3)x⁴ + … A1
METHOD 2: (M1) attempt to find Maclaurin series for e^(−2x²) OR e^(2x⁴/3); A1 for correct substitution and product; A1 for final series 1 − 2x² + (8/3)x⁴ + …

blocks.task_summary: Use the first two non-zero terms in the Maclaurin series for f(x) to show that ∫₀^(1/10) e^(cos 2x) dx ≈ 149e/1500.
method_path: substitute f(x) ≈ e(1 − 2x²) into the definite integral
integrate term by term: ∫ e(1 − 2x²) dx = e[x − 2x³/3]
simplify to 298e/3000 = 149e/1500

evidence.basis: (M1) ∫₀^(1/10) e^(cos2x) dx ≈ ∫₀^(1/10) e(1 − 2x²) dx; A1 for [e(x − 2x³/3)]₀^(1/10); A1 e(1/10 − 2/3000) = 298e/3000 = 149e/1500 AG. Note: if candidate follows through an incorrect expansion from part (d), award a maximum of M1A1FTA0.
